subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
skillName: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: End-of-cluster mastery check for 7.SP.A: using random sampling to draw inferences about a population. Twelve multiple-choice questions, six per standard. The first six items cover statistical sampling (7.SP.A.1) and the last six cover drawing inferences from samples (7.SP.A.2).

items.prompt:
A principal wants to know the favorite lunch of all $850$ students at her school. She surveys $50$ of them. What is the population in this study?
A) The $50$ students who were surveyed
B) All $850$ students at the school
C) The principal
D) The favorite lunch choices
items.answer: B) All $850$ students at the school

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about, here all $850$ students.
So B is correct.
A names the sample (the subset actually surveyed), not the population.
C is the person doing the survey, not a group being studied.
D names the variable being measured, not the group of people.
solution.answer: B) All $850$ students at the school

items.prompt:
To learn about the reading habits of all $1200$ students in a district, a researcher draws $80$ student ID numbers from a hat and surveys those students. Which group is the sample?
A) All $1200$ students in the district
B) The $80$ students whose IDs were drawn
C) The reading habits being studied
D) The hat of ID numbers
items.answer: B) The $80$ students whose IDs were drawn

steps: A sample is the subset of the population that is actually examined.
Here the $80$ students who were drawn and surveyed are the sample, so B is correct.
A names the whole population, not the sample.
C is the variable being measured, not a group of people.
D is the tool used to select the sample, not the sample itself.
solution.answer: B) The $80$ students whose IDs were drawn

items.prompt:
Which sampling method gives every member of a population an equal chance of being chosen?
A) Surveying the first $20$ people who walk by
B) Asking volunteers to email their opinions
C) Drawing names randomly from a list of everyone in the population
D) Surveying only members of the chess club
items.answer: C) Drawing names randomly from a list of everyone in the population

steps: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection.
Drawing names randomly from a complete list does exactly that, so C is correct.
A is a convenience sample, only people who happen to walk by can be chosen.
B is a voluntary-response sample, only people who choose to reply are included.
D samples one subgroup, so most of the population has no chance of being picked.
solution.answer: C) Drawing names randomly from a list of everyone in the population

items.prompt:
A reporter interviews the first $25$ people leaving a movie theater to find out how the whole town feels about the film. How is this sample best classified?
A) A simple random sample
B) A convenience sample
C) A representative sample
D) A systematic sample of the town

steps: The reporter chose whoever was easiest to reach, the first people leaving, so this is a convenience sample. B is correct.
A is wrong because the townspeople did not each have an equal chance, only theater-goers could be picked.
C is wrong because moviegoers who just saw this film are not representative of the whole town.
D is wrong because systematic sampling means choosing at a fixed interval (such as every $10$th person) from the full population, which is not what happened.

items.prompt:
To learn how all city residents get to work, a researcher surveys only people waiting at a downtown bus stop. Why is this sample biased?
A) The sample size is too small to mean anything
B) It overrepresents bus riders and misses people who drive, walk, or bike
C) Bus stops are never crowded enough to survey
D) It is biased only if fewer than $100$ people are surveyed
items.answer: B) It overrepresents bus riders and misses people who drive, walk, or bike

steps: People at a bus stop are far more likely to commute by bus than the average resident.
This location bias overrepresents bus riders and leaves out drivers, walkers, and cyclists, so the sample is not representative. B is correct.
A is wrong because the flaw is who was sampled, not how many; even a huge bus-stop sample stays biased.
C is an irrelevant claim about crowding.
D is wrong because bias comes from the selection method, not from crossing some size threshold.
solution.answer: B) It overrepresents bus riders and misses people who drive, walk, or bike

items.prompt:
A company posts an online poll asking customers to rate a product and gets $5000$ responses, mostly from people who were unhappy and wanted to complain. A manager says the large number of responses makes the result trustworthy. Which statement is correct?
A) The manager is right, $5000$ responses is large enough to be representative
B) The sample is still biased because it is self-selected; size does not fix bias
C) The poll is unbiased because everyone had the chance to respond
D) The result is valid only because it was collected online
items.answer: B) The sample is still biased because it is self-selected; size does not fix bias

steps: A voluntary online poll is a self-selected (voluntary-response) sample: only people motivated to respond are counted, here mostly unhappy customers.
A large sample size does not remove this bias, so the result is not representative. B is correct.
A is the misconception that a big sample is automatically representative; a biased method stays biased no matter the size.
C is wrong because having the chance to respond is not the same as being randomly selected; the people who respond differ systematically from those who do not.
D is wrong because being collected online does not make a self-selected sample valid.
solution.answer: B) The sample is still biased because it is self-selected; size does not fix bias

items.prompt:
In a random sample of $20$ of the $200$ marbles in a bag, $5$ are red. About how many of the $200$ marbles are red?
A) $5$
B) $25$
C) $50$
D) $40$

steps: The sample proportion of red marbles is $\frac{5}{20} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Scale up to the population of $200$: $\frac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$. So C is correct.
A reports the raw sample count $5$ without scaling up.
B comes from multiplying $5 \times 5$ or scaling by the sample size instead of the population.
D does not match any correct proportional calculation here.

items.prompt:
In a random sample of $40$ books in a library, $\frac{3}{10}$ are nonfiction. The library has $500$ books. About how many are nonfiction?
A) $30$
B) $150$
C) $12$
D) $470$

steps: The sample proportion of nonfiction is $\frac{3}{10}$.
Scale up to the $500$ books: $\frac{3}{10} \times 500 = 150$. So B is correct.
A comes from multiplying by the wrong base.
C reports the sample count $\frac{3}{10} \times 40 = 12$ instead of scaling to the population.
D estimates the fiction books, $500 - 30$ style errors, not the nonfiction count.

items.prompt:
In a random sample of $80$ light bulbs from a large shipment, $6$ are defective. Estimate the percent of all bulbs in the shipment that are defective.
A) $6\%$
B) $7.5\%$
C) $13.3\%$
D) $0.75\%$

steps: The sample proportion defective is $\frac{6}{80}$.
Convert to a percent: $\frac{6}{80} = 0.075 = 7.5\%$. So B is correct.
A reports the raw count $6$ read as a percent, ignoring the base of $80$.
C inverts the ratio, computing $\frac{80}{6}$ style or otherwise misplacing the numbers.
D misplaces the decimal point, giving a tenth of the correct value.

items.prompt:
In a random sample of $40$ students, $14$ said they walk to school. The school has $600$ students. Estimate how many students in the whole school walk to school.
A) $14$
B) $210$
C) $560$
D) $1714$

steps: The sample proportion who walk is $\frac{14}{40}$.
Scale up to $600$ students: $\frac{14}{40} \times 600 = 14 \times 15 = 210$. So B is correct.
A reports the raw sample count $14$ without scaling up.
C estimates the number who do NOT walk by mixing the sample size with the population, computing $600 - 40 = 560$ instead of applying the proportion.
D inverts the proportion, computing $\frac{40}{14} \times 600 \approx 1714$ instead of $\frac{14}{40} \times 600$.

items.prompt:
Four random samples of $50$ voters each gave the percent favoring a measure as $46\%$, $52\%$, $48\%$, and $54\%$. Using all four samples, which is the best estimate of the percent of all voters who favor the measure, with a reasonable range?
A) Exactly $46\%$, since that was one of the samples
B) About $50\%$, with a reasonable range of $46\%$ to $54\%$
C) $200\%$, the sum of the four percents
D) Exactly $54\%$, since larger estimates are more reliable
items.answer: B) About $50\%$, with a reasonable range of $46\%$ to $54\%$

steps: Average the four sample percents: $\frac{46 + 52 + 48 + 54}{4} = \frac{200}{4} = 50\%$.
The samples vary from a low of $46\%$ to a high of $54\%$, so a reasonable range for the true value is $46\%$ to $54\%$. B is correct.
A picks a single sample and ignores the variation across the others.
C adds the percents instead of averaging them, giving an impossible $200\%$.
D wrongly assumes the largest estimate is the most reliable; no single sample is the true value.
solution.answer: B) About $50\%$, with a reasonable range of $46\%$ to $54\%$

items.prompt:
To estimate the favorite sport of all students at a school, Maria surveys only members of the basketball team and concludes basketball is the most popular sport school-wide. What is the best evaluation of her conclusion?
A) Valid, because she surveyed real students
B) Valid, because the basketball team is a large group
C) Not valid, because the basketball team is not representative and overstates interest in basketball
D) Not valid only because she did not survey enough players
items.answer: C) Not valid, because the basketball team is not representative and overstates interest in basketball

steps: Maria's sample is the basketball team, a group already chosen for liking basketball, so it is not representative of all students.
Her estimate is biased and overstates interest in basketball, so the inference is not valid. C is correct.
A is wrong because surveying real students does not make a biased sample representative.
B is the misconception that a large or biased group is automatically accurate; representativeness, not size, is the issue.
D is wrong because the flaw is who was sampled, not how many; surveying more basketball players would not fix the bias.
solution.answer: C) Not valid, because the basketball team is not representative and overstates interest in basketball
